sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Bergen County
sections.html:
Your town does. Bergen County is split into 70 municipalities (56 boroughs, nine townships, three cities and two villages), more than any other New Jersey county, and each one assesses its own parcels and collects its own tax. The county has one tax body, the Bergen County Board of Taxation, which sits at Two Bergen County Plaza, 1st Floor, Hackensack, and takes assessment appeals. Its number is 201-336-6300. The county website also hosts a property record search and the board's meeting schedule.

Oakland and Mahwah fall inside the Highlands preservation area, where extra state rules from a 2004 water protection law apply. A seller there should ask the town what limits a buyer might face.

Bergen has the largest population of any New Jersey county, with an estimated 977,026 people in 2025. It is a costly, owner-heavy market.

  • Half of owned homes are worth more than $623,000.
  • The middle household earns $124,884 a year.
  • Owners occupy 65.3 percent of households.
  • Owners with a mortgage pay a median $3,547 a month, and those without pay $1,498.
  • Rent runs $1,914 a month.

The county holds the northern ends of the New Jersey Turnpike and Garden State Parkway, the eastern end of Interstate 80 and a stretch of Interstate 287, and the George Washington Bridge ties Fort Lee to Upper Manhattan. The mean commute is 31.2 minutes, so access to highways and buses is part of how a house gets priced.

Petitions go to the Bergen County Board of Taxation, which asks filers to use its online system. The cutoff is April 1, or 45 days after bulk assessment notices go out, and moves to May 1 when a town has revalued. Mark the date each spring, because a late petition is not heard.

Bergen County appeal checkpoints
CheckpointRule
Valuation dateOctober 1 before the tax year
Petition dueApril 1, or May 1 after a revaluation
Proof attachedSales of 3 to 5 comparable properties
Copies to assessor and board7 days before the hearing
DecisionWithin 3 months of the due date
Value freezeThe appeal year and the 2 after it

Today's assessment is presumed right. You must show it exceeds market value, and a bill cannot be appealed just because the tax rises with the local budget.

sections.h2: What proof helps at a hearing
sections.html:
The state wants market value on the October 1 valuation date, supported by sales that closed before that day. Assessments of similar houses are not accepted as proof.

  • Three to five recent sales of homes like yours.
  • Photos of your house and each comparable.
  • An income statement, for commercial property.
  • An appraisal or repair estimate where the house has flaws.

Attend the hearing. The board rarely grants delays, and missing it can produce a judgment for lack of prosecution that closes the door on the Tax Court of New Jersey. Where a town has not revalued lately, the board also measures your assessment against a band of 15 percent either side of the district's average ratio.

Request a payoff from your town's tax collector, not the county. The title company or closing attorney wants to know which quarterly installments are paid and what interest is owed. Quarters commonly fall on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, and your own collector will confirm local dates.

  • Ask your attorney how the contract splits the quarter in which you close.
  • Report any addition you built, since added assessments can create an extra bill.
  • If an appeal is still pending, decide in the contract who gets any refund.

Back taxes and interest are paid out of the seller's share at closing, so get the payoff figure before you fix a closing date. A balance that is a quarter or two behind does not stop a sale. It only changes the number on the settlement statement.

Older residents and disabled owners may qualify for a $250 deduction through Form PTD, renewed each year with Form PD5 by March 1. The Division of Taxation's Property Administration unit takes questions at 609-292-7974 or 609-292-7975. If you hold the deduction and you are selling mid-year, tell your closing agent so the proration is based on the right amount.

Some Bergen County owners cannot wait for a listing, an appraisal and a buyer's mortgage. An inherited house, a pending move or a stack of tax notices can make a firm date worth more than a top price. In a cash sale, the buyer skips financing and takes the house as-is, so repairs and showings drop away.

The tax work does not disappear. Order a collector payoff, check for open permits or unreported additions, and sort out who gets any appeal refund. Those three steps cover most of the questions a title company will ask.

sections.h2: Steps to take before you list
sections.html:
Start with three calls. Ask your town's tax collector for a payoff and the dates of your quarterly installments. Ask the assessor for your property record card and compare it with the house as it stands today. Then ask the Board of Taxation whether your town has revalued recently, since that decides whether your petition date is April 1 or May 1.

With those answers you can decide whether an appeal is worth filing before you sell or whether the closing date matters more. A pending appeal can be carried into a sale, as long as the contract says who receives any refund.

Bring the same packet you filed: three to five comparable sales, photos and any appraisal or repair estimate. The board looks at what the house was worth on the October 1 valuation date, not at what the neighbors pay in tax. Copies of your evidence must reach the assessor and the board seven days ahead, so build that into your schedule.

A decision is due within three months of the petition deadline. If the board lowers your value, the new figure is frozen for the appeal year and the two years after it, unless something such as a revaluation changes it. If you lose, the Tax Court of New Jersey is the next step, and a missed hearing can end that option.

The notice lists the assessed value for the land and the buildings. Check the lot size, the square footage, the number of rooms and any finished basement against what you own. A simple error on the record card is one of the easiest ways to win a reduction. Photos of damage, a failing roof or a flooded basement help show that the house is worth less than the card assumes.

Remember that the tax bill itself cannot be appealed. Only the value can, and the comparison the board cares about is market value against assessment.

faqs.q: Who is paid the property tax in Bergen County?
faqs.a: The tax collector of your own municipality, not the county. All 70 towns run their own billing and payment methods, and the county board in Hackensack hears only assessment appeals.

faqs.q: By when must a Bergen County owner petition against an assessment?
faqs.a: By April 1 of the tax year, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of notices. Where a town revalued, the date is May 1.

faqs.q: Where can a Bergen County owner reach the Board of Taxation?
faqs.a: The office is at Two Bergen County Plaza, 1st Floor, in Hackensack, and the number is 201-336-6300. In person filing is accepted, though the county prefers online petitions.

faqs.q: What if a Bergen County owner skips the tax hearing?
faqs.a: The board can enter a judgment for lack of prosecution, which can bar a later appeal to the Tax Court. Adjournments are normally denied.

faqs.q: Can a Bergen County house sell while a tax quarter is unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes and interest are paid from the seller's share at closing, using the payoff the municipal collector supplies. Get that figure before you fix a closing date.
